name: Kobuk Valley National Park
blurb: Caribou, lichen and wolves where the Arctic taiga meets the tundra.

tip.title: Stop the caribou migration
tip.text: Caribou feed wolves, wolverines, ravens and bears. Set Caribou to -100% and watch the predators and scavengers, while lichen and willow recover.

sources.title: NPS: Kobuk Valley nature and science

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Kobuk Valley National Park, Reindeer, Wolverine). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: A pale lichen carpeting the woodland floor. Wikipedia calls lichens a staple for caribou in winter, which dig through snow to reach them.
Shrubby willows grow along the Kobuk and on the tundra edge. Moose browse their shoots and caribou also feed on them.
Grass-like plants of wet tundra and river flats, among the most recorded plants near the park.
Around 400,000 caribou of the Western Arctic herd cross the Kobuk River each year between winter and calving grounds. They feed on lichen in winter.
Browses willow shoots and twigs in winter and eats forbs and aquatic plants in summer. Wolves, bears and wolverines all use it.
A small rodent of damp tundra and river flats, and a staple prey of foxes, wolves and bears in GloBI records.
A tundra rodent that eats sedges and other low plants. Lemmings undergo large swings in numbers, which ripple up to their predators.
Mainly a scavenger that relies on carrion, often from wolf kills, but also hunts small mammals and sometimes weakened large animals.
Listed by the park service among its predators. A small hunter of voles and lemmings.
A year-round scavenger that feeds on carrion at carcasses left by larger predators.
Wolf packs hunt caribou and moose in the park, and their kills feed wolverines, ravens and bears.
An omnivore that takes moose calves and small rodents, and often scavenges wolf kills.

nodes.name: Fungi & soil microbes
nodes.desc: Slowly break down dead plants and carcasses in the cold soil and return nutrients to it.

story: Kobuk Valley National Park lies about 25 miles north of the Arctic Circle in northwestern Alaska. It was set aside in 1980 to protect the 100-foot Great Kobuk Sand Dunes and caribou migration routes. It covers 1,750,716 acres and has no roads or designated trails.
matters: It is one of the least-visited national parks, reached only by chartered air taxi. Tundra caribou are adapted for extreme cold, and some herds make long-distance migrations.
